'Before we pay the token amount, let's have the papers checked,' said Chaitanya.
'The agent says there's no need. Two other buyers are waiting.'
'Then two other buyers can take the risk. I've booked a lawyer for Thursday to look over the title papers and the approvals.'
'And the bank?'
'I'm calling tomorrow to ask what we're eligible for, so we don't fall in love with something we can't borrow for.'
Nilesh nodded slowly. 'It feels a bit like distrusting the seller.'
'It's not distrust. It's knowing what we're signing. If everything's fine, we've lost a week.'
'And if it isn't?'
'Then we've saved far more than a week.'
On Friday the lawyer said the papers were in order except for one approval that needed clarifying. The seller sorted it out in a few days.

The builder's office in Ernakulam wanted a token amount that same afternoon. "Two other families are interested," the sales manager said.
Anitha squeezed my hand. The flat was right. But my father had told me stories of people losing everything over bad papers.
So I said, "We'll come back on Monday."
That weekend we did two things. First, we took copies of the title documents and building approvals to Baljeet, a property lawyer a colleague recommended. Baljeet went through them page by page and asked the builder for one missing approval certificate.
Second, we visited our bank to check what loan we were actually eligible for and whether the bank would finance this project at all.
On Monday, the certificate had come through and the bank confirmed. We paid the token then, calm, not rushed. The other two families never appeared.
— Jomon

qa.a: Baljeet, a property lawyer a colleague recommended.

qa.a: Jomon felt pressured and a little worried, remembering stories of people losing everything over bad papers.

qa.q: What else could Jomon and Anitha check before paying?
qa.a: They could compare the flat with their must-have list and visit at different times of day to check the commute and surroundings.

qa.q: How might Anitha have felt paying the token on Monday?
qa.a: Anitha probably felt calm and reassured, knowing the papers and loan had been checked by professionals.

Lawyer's note — file for Nikita and Aniket, flat in Kharadi. Written by Jasleen.

The couple came to my office on a Tuesday, three days before they planned to pay a token amount. Nikita brought a folder: sale agreement draft, title documents going back thirty years, building plan approval, and the builder's completion schedule.
She was clear about why they'd come. "We don't know what to look for. We just want someone qualified to check before we pay anything."
I went through the file over two days. One land-use document was an old copy; I asked for the updated one. Everything else was in order.
Meanwhile, Aniket had visited their bank with salary slips and got a written note on loan eligibility and whether the bank had approved the project.
On Friday I confirmed the papers were in order. They paid the token that afternoon.
My note to self: this is how every buyer should come in, with time to check and no rush.

qa.q: How many years of title documents did Nikita bring?
qa.a: Title documents going back thirty years.

qa.q: How did Nikita seem to feel about checking the papers?
qa.a: Nikita seemed cautious and a little unsure, knowing they didn't know what to look for, but calmer once someone qualified checked.

qa.q: What else could Nikita and Aniket do before the final sale?
qa.a: They could keep checking with the lawyer at each step, such as before the final agreement, and stick to their budget and must-haves.

qa.q: How does the couple's approach look to the lawyer?
qa.a: The lawyer sees them as an example of doing it properly, arriving with time to check rather than in a rush.

grounding: It shows a couple asking a lawyer to check title papers and approvals and speaking to a bank about eligibility before paying a token amount.
